lessons.title: What ovarian reserve testing measures
lessons.objective: Tell oocyte quantity apart from reproductive potential and know what AMH and AFC are useful for in stimulation.
lessons.closing: AMH and AFC count; they are not good independent predictors of pregnancy. Their territory is anticipating how many oocytes will respond to stimulation.

lessons.title: AMH and natural fertility
lessons.objective: Interpret the evidence that AMH does not predict spontaneous conception and explain it to patients.
lessons.closing: In women without known infertility, a low AMH did not foretell fewer conceptions (positive test). Ordering it “to know whether I can wait” does not answer that question.

lessons.title: Responsible use: don't deny, don't sell, don't over-order
lessons.objective: Avoid inappropriate uses of reserve markers: denying treatment, promoting egg freezing and ordering obsolete dynamic tests.
lessons.closing: A lab number guides counselling; on its own it does not decide who gets treatment or who freezes eggs.

items.title: AMH and AFC measure quantity, not quality
items.core: Ovarian reserve markers estimate how many follicles remain; their relation to oocyte quality and live birth is weak or inconsistent. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
The antral follicle count (AFC) is the sum of antral follicles in both ovaries on transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase; most studies define them as 2–10 mm in mean diameter. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

AMH is produced by granulosa cells of growing follicles, so it tracks the size of the follicle pool. Neither marker tells you about the competence of each oocyte.
items.recall: What does AMH tell you, and what doesn't it?

rows.text: Oocyte quality and live birth: weak or inconsistent relation

visual.alt: Diagram: AMH and AFC reflect follicle number; their relation to oocyte quality and live birth is weak or inconsistent.

items.application: When reporting an AMH, explicitly separate “how many” from “how good”: it is a common confusion.

items.title: Before interpreting an AMH: what changes it
items.core: AMH may be suppressed by current or recent combined oral contraceptive use (the guideline also lists ovarian surgery among the factors to consider); in addition, its level depends on age and BMI and may vary across the cycle. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
According to the practice points of the 2023 international PCOS guideline: in the general population AMH peaks around ages 20–25 and is lower with higher BMI; it may be suppressed by current or recent combined oral contraceptive use, and the guideline also lists ovarian surgery among the factors to consider; and it may vary across the cycle. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

Laboratories should use population- and assay-specific cut-offs: an AMH that is “low by the lab range” cannot be compared directly with figures from another assay. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Which factors can lower or alter an AMH, and what should you check about the lab?
items.application: Before interpreting an AMH, ask about recent hormonal contraception and ovarian surgery, and check which assay and cut-off the lab used.

items.title: What they are for: predicting response to stimulation
items.core: ESHRE recommends using AFC or AMH to predict a high or low response to ovarian stimulation. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.body:
Reserve markers are good predictors of the number of oocytes retrieved in IVF. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

By contrast, the ESHRE guideline does not recommend using age, BMI, basal FSH, inhibin B, basal oestradiol, basal progesterone or basal LH to predict response (strong recommendation). [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]] In short: to anticipate response, AFC or AMH; not a panel of basal hormones.
items.recall: Which marker does ESHRE recommend to predict response to stimulation?
items.application: If a patient is going to stimulation, AMH or AFC help anticipate low or high response and counsel on risks; adding inhibin B or FSH is not needed for that.
items.pearl: AFC or AMH, depending on context: ESHRE recommends either one to stratify response. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]

items.title: Myth: “low AMH = IVF won't work”
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend AFC, AMH or other basal markers to predict pregnancy or live birth; female age and BMI, by contrast, are predictors. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.body:
According to ASRM, AMH as an independent variable is at best weakly predictive of pregnancy. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

NICE takes a different nuance: it recommends using AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] This is not a head-on contradiction: fewer oocytes means fewer cumulative opportunities, but it does not say which will be competent and does not mean “it won’t work”.
items.recall: Is AMH useful to forecast live birth in IVF?
items.pearl: Always distinguish the outcome: oocytes retrieved (biomarker) ≠ clinical pregnancy ≠ live birth.

items.title: Key study: low AMH did not predict fewer conceptions
items.core: In women aged 30–44 without known infertility, AMH <0.7 ng/mL was not associated with a lower probability of conceiving by 6 or 12 cycles. [[ref:steiner-2017-jama]]
items.body:
Prospective cohort: 981 women enrolled and 750 analysed, trying to conceive for ≤3 months. Adjusted probability of conceiving with AMH <0.7 ng/mL versus normal AMH: 65% vs 62% by 6 cycles and 84% vs 75% by 12 cycles, with no significant differences. The low-AMH subgroup was small (84 women) and its confidence interval wide (50–75% by 6 cycles). High FSH was not associated with lower fertility either. [[ref:steiner-2017-jama]]

Mind the outcome: “conception” was a positive pregnancy test, not a live birth. And it does not apply to women with already diagnosed infertility.
items.recall: What did Steiner 2017 find about low AMH and the chance of conceiving?

visual.alt: Adjusted probability of conceiving with AMH below 0.7 ng/mL versus normal: 65% versus 62% by 6 cycles and 84% versus 75% by 12 cycles; no significant difference.

items.application: Useful to reassure, with data, a woman without infertility who brings a low AMH from a check-up; reassurance does not change the weight of age or time trying.

evidence.label: association
evidence.note: Prospective cohort: association, not a trial.

items.title: What I would not order: reserve testing to forecast spontaneous pregnancy
items.core: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the cause of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
It is a strong ESHRE recommendation with low certainty of evidence: strength and certainty are different things. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

ASRM agrees: the markers do not predict current reproductive potential in women of unproven fertility, and in women with infertility they are not useful to predict unassisted pregnancy. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]] NICE concurs: do not use AMH to predict pregnancy through spontaneous conception. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: In a woman with regular cycles, is AMH needed to work up the cause of her infertility?
items.pearl: A recommendation can be strong even with low-certainty evidence when the balance of benefit, harm and cost is clear.

items.title: Patient phrase: “Does my AMH tell me if I can wait?”
items.core: Reserve markers should not be used as a fertility test. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
Suggested answer: “AMH estimates how many eggs would respond to treatment, but it does not predict when you will get pregnant or whether you can wait. In women without fertility problems, a low AMH was not associated with fewer pregnancies.” [[ref:steiner-2017-jama]]

Then discuss what does matter for her plan: age, time trying, cycles, history and assessment of the partner.
items.recall: How would you explain to a patient what her AMH can and cannot tell her?
items.application: Prevents an isolated number from causing distress or rushed decisions.

items.title: A very low AMH does not justify refusing IVF
items.core: Extremely low AMH values should not be used to refuse IVF treatment. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
ASRM is explicit: reserve markers should not be used to deny access to infertility treatment. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

They do help with counselling: with very low reserve fewer oocytes are expected, and that information supports shared decisions about expectations and alternatives.
items.recall: Can a very low AMH alone be a reason to refuse IVF?

items.title: Don't use AMH to promote egg freezing
items.core: Ovarian reserve markers should not be used to promote planned oocyte cryopreservation. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
The reasoning follows from the above: if AMH does not predict current reproductive potential, it cannot indicate who “needs” to freeze. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

The decision to freeze is discussed from the person's reproductive plans and realistic information about the technique, not from a lab value used as an alarm.
items.recall: Should a low AMH be used to recommend egg freezing?

items.title: Tests to drop: clomiphene challenge and isolated FSH
items.core: Dynamic tests such as the clomiphene citrate challenge test do not improve prediction of poor response over basal markers and should be abandoned. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
An elevated basal FSH is specific but not sensitive for diminished ovarian reserve: if high it is informative, but a normal FSH does not rule it out. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

That is why, when reserve truly needs estimating (for example, before stimulation), AFC or AMH are preferred. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.recall: What is the limitation of a normal basal FSH for ruling out low reserve?

items.stem: Which of these outcomes does AMH predict best?

options.text: The number of oocytes retrieved in IVF stimulation.
options.why: Correct: reserve markers are good predictors of oocyte yield.

options.text: The probability of live birth after IVF.
options.why: AMH is at best weakly predictive of pregnancy; ESHRE advises against using it to predict live birth.

options.text: The probability of spontaneous pregnancy within 6 months.
options.why: In women without infertility, a low AMH was not associated with a lower chance of conceiving.

options.text: The quality of each oocyte.
options.why: AMH reflects quantity; its association with oocyte quality is weak.

items.explanation: AMH and AFC count follicles: their strength is anticipating how many oocytes will be retrieved.

items.stem: Before IVF stimulation, what does ESHRE recommend to predict a high or low response?

options.text: Basal inhibin B.
options.why: ESHRE lists it among the markers it does not recommend for predicting response.

options.text: AFC or AMH.
options.why: Correct: this is the ESHRE guideline recommendation.

options.text: Combined basal FSH and oestradiol.
options.why: Both are among the markers ESHRE does not recommend for predicting response.

options.text: Age and BMI.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend using them to predict ovarian response.

items.explanation: To anticipate response: AFC or AMH. Not a panel of basal hormones.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman, trying to conceive for 2 months, regular cycles, no history. She brings a low AMH from a check-up. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Her chance of spontaneous pregnancy within 6 months is clearly reduced.
options.why: In the Steiner (2017) cohort, a low AMH was not associated with a lower chance of conceiving in this population.

options.text: AMH alone does not predict her spontaneous conception; it would inform response if she ever needed stimulation.
options.why: Correct: it separates what AMH measures (follicle pool) from what it did not predict (fecundability).

options.text: She should start IVF immediately because of the low AMH.
options.why: AMH is not a fertility test: on its own it does not justify recommending IVF.

options.text: The low AMH indicates poorer oocyte quality.
options.why: AMH reflects follicle number; its relation to oocyte quality is weak or inconsistent.

items.explanation: What weighs in her plan is age, time trying and clinical assessment of the couple, not the AMH figure.

items.stem: In the Steiner et al. cohort (JAMA 2017), how was “conception” defined?

options.text: Live birth.
options.why: The study did not measure live births, so it cannot be extrapolated directly to that outcome.

options.text: Clinical pregnancy with heartbeat on ultrasound.
options.why: This was not the study outcome.

options.text: A positive pregnancy test.
options.why: Correct: an early outcome, different from clinical pregnancy and live birth.

options.text: Ongoing pregnancy at 12 weeks.
options.why: This was not the study outcome.

items.explanation: Reading the exact outcome is part of critical appraisal: biomarker, positive test, clinical pregnancy and live birth are not interchangeable.

items.stem: ESHRE (2023) states that, with regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to predict spontaneous conception. How is that recommendation graded?

options.text: Strong, with low certainty of evidence.
options.why: Correct: recommendation strength and evidence certainty are graded separately.

options.text: Strong, with high certainty.
options.why: The certainty assigned was low.

options.text: Conditional, with low certainty.
options.why: The recommendation is strong, not conditional.

options.text: Good practice point, no evidence.
options.why: It is an evidence-based recommendation with graded certainty.

items.explanation: A recommendation can be strong with low-certainty evidence when the balance of benefits, harms and costs is clear.

items.stem: A couple with an indication for IVF has an extremely low AMH. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Refuse IVF because there is no point trying.
options.why: ASRM: extremely low AMH values should not be used to refuse IVF.

options.text: Counsel on the expected response (fewer oocytes) and decide together, without using AMH as an exclusion criterion.
options.why: Correct: AMH informs counselling, not access.

options.text: Refer straight to egg donation without counselling on other options.
options.why: Using AMH to rule out treatment with her own oocytes without counselling amounts to denying access based on a marker, which ASRM advises against.

options.text: Do a clomiphene challenge test to confirm.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve accuracy and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: Reserve markers should not be used to deny access to infertility treatment.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with no current wish to conceive asks for an AMH “to decide whether to freeze my eggs”. What would you answer?

options.text: That if the AMH is low, she should freeze as soon as possible.
options.why: Reserve markers should not be used to promote planned freezing.

options.text: That AMH does not indicate who needs to freeze; the decision is discussed based on her reproductive plans and realistic information.
options.why: Correct: consistent with ASRM 2020.

options.text: That with a normal AMH she can postpone pregnancy without risk.
options.why: AMH does not predict reproductive potential; a normal AMH does not guarantee future fertility.

options.text: That a clomiphene challenge test in addition to AMH would help.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve accuracy and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: A low AMH does not mandate freezing, and a normal AMH does not make waiting risk-free.

items.stem: Regarding basal FSH as a marker of diminished ovarian reserve, which statement is correct?

options.text: It is sensitive: a normal FSH rules out low reserve.
options.why: It is not sensitive: a normal FSH does not rule it out.

options.text: It is specific but not sensitive.
options.why: Correct: if elevated it is informative, but if normal it does not rule out.

options.text: Its accuracy improves with a clomiphene challenge test.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve accuracy over basal markers.

options.text: It is the marker ESHRE recommends to predict response.
options.why: ESHRE recommends AFC or AMH, not basal FSH.

items.explanation: To estimate reserve when needed, AFC or AMH; isolated FSH does not rule out and the clomiphene test should be abandoned.

items.stem: How do most studies define the antral follicle count (AFC)?

options.text: Follicles of 10–20 mm in the ovary with the dominant follicle, at mid-cycle.
options.why: AFC sums both ovaries, counts 2–10 mm follicles and is done in the early follicular phase.

options.text: 2–10 mm follicles in both ovaries, in the mid-luteal phase.
options.why: The size is right but the timing is not: AFC is done in the early follicular phase.

options.text: Sum of 2–10 mm (mean diameter) follicles in both ovaries, on transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase.
options.why: Correct: this is the definition reported by ASRM.

options.text: Any visible follicle in one ovary, multiplied by two.
options.why: AFC is the actual sum of both ovaries, with a defined size range (2–10 mm).

items.explanation: AFC: both ovaries, 2–10 mm follicles, transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase. Like AMH, it estimates quantity, not quality.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with an AMH in the upper part of the range asks: “So my eggs are good quality?” Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: AMH reflects how many follicles remain; it does not tell you about the quality of each oocyte.
options.why: Correct: it separates “how many” from “how good”.

options.text: Yes: a high AMH indicates good-quality oocytes.
options.why: This is the common confusion to avoid: AMH tracks pool size, not the competence of each oocyte.

options.text: Yes, as long as the AFC is also high.
options.why: AFC also measures quantity; adding both does not turn them into quality markers.

options.text: No: a high AMH indicates poorer oocyte quality.
options.why: Not in the reverse direction either: the relation of these markers to quality is weak or inconsistent.

items.explanation: AMH is produced by granulosa cells of growing follicles: it follows pool size. Its relation to oocyte quality and live birth is weak or inconsistent.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman stopped a combined oral contraceptive 4 weeks ago. She brings an AMH “low by the lab range”. What is the most prudent interpretation?

options.text: It confirms diminished ovarian reserve.
options.why: It cannot confirm that: current or recent combined contraceptive use may suppress AMH.

options.text: Contraceptives do not change AMH, so the result is reliable.
options.why: False: the guideline notes AMH may be suppressed by current or recent combined contraception.

options.text: It indicates she should freeze eggs as soon as possible.
options.why: Besides the contraceptive factor, reserve markers should not be used to promote egg freezing.

options.text: AMH may be suppressed by the recent combined contraceptive use; it must be interpreted in that context.
options.why: Correct: it is one of the factors the 2023 PCOS guideline asks you to consider.

items.explanation: Before interpreting an AMH, ask about current or recent combined hormonal contraception and check the lab’s assay and cut-off: the 2023 PCOS guideline asks for population- and assay-specific cut-offs.

items.stem: According to the practice points of the 2023 international PCOS guideline, which statement about AMH in the general population is correct?

options.text: It peaks around ages 30–35.
options.why: The peak is around ages 20–25.

options.text: It is lower with a higher BMI.
options.why: Correct: the guideline states AMH is lower with higher BMI.

options.text: It is stable across the menstrual cycle.
options.why: The guideline states it may vary across the cycle.

options.text: It can be compared directly between different assays.
options.why: Laboratories should use population- and assay-specific cut-offs.

items.explanation: Factors that modify AMH: age (peak around 20–25), BMI (lower with higher BMI), current or recent combined oral contraceptives and variation across the cycle. Cut-offs should be population- and assay-specific.

items.stem: A patient brings an AMH measured in one laboratory and you want to classify it with a cut-off published for a different assay. What is correct?

options.text: Apply the published cut-off: AMH is the same across all assays.
options.why: The guideline asks for assay-specific cut-offs; figures from different assays are not compared directly.

options.text: Convert it to basal FSH to compare it.
options.why: No such conversion exists; besides, basal FSH is not recommended to predict ovarian response.

options.text: Interpret it with that laboratory’s population- and assay-specific cut-off.
options.why: Correct: this is practice point 1.5.7 of the 2023 PCOS guideline.

options.text: Always repeat it with a clomiphene challenge test.
options.why: Dynamic tests such as the clomiphene challenge do not improve prediction and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: An AMH that is “low by the lab range” cannot be compared directly with figures from another assay. ESHRE adds that because studies used different assays and ranges, common cut-offs for low or high response could not be calculated.

items.stem: A clinic proposes always measuring both AFC and AMH before ovarian stimulation “to refine prediction”. Which approach is consistent with the ESHRE 2025 guideline?

options.text: Use AFC or AMH, choosing the test best suited to the clinical setting.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation; the clinician decides which is most appropriate in their setting.

options.text: Always measure AFC and AMH together, because combining them improves prediction.
options.why: ESHRE cites data that combining them did not improve response prediction.

options.text: Add basal FSH and inhibin B to refine prediction.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend using basal FSH or inhibin B to predict response.

options.text: Use age alone, which is sufficiently reliable.
options.why: Age has some predictive value, but ESHRE considers it not reliable enough on its own to classify response.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2025: AFC or AMH (strong) to predict high or low response; not age, BMI, basal FSH, inhibin B, oestradiol, progesterone or basal LH.

items.stem: Basal FSH and inhibin B have some predictive value for ovarian response. Why does ESHRE 2025 still not recommend using them for that purpose?

options.text: Because they can only be measured in the luteal phase.
options.why: That is not the guideline’s argument; the problem is their limited clinical value compared with AFC and AMH.

options.text: Because they predict live birth better than response.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend them for predicting pregnancy or live birth either.

options.text: Because they have no relation at all to ovarian response.
options.why: The guideline acknowledges some predictive value; what is lacking is clinical usefulness at realistic cut-offs.

options.text: Because accurate prediction needs very high cut-offs that very few women reach, and more accurate tests exist.
options.why: Correct: that is ESHRE’s justification: they have hardly any clinical value.

items.explanation: ESHRE: the accuracy of basal FSH and inhibin B is moderate; good prediction needs very high cut-offs, so they have hardly any clinical value compared with AFC or AMH.

items.stem: According to ESHRE 2025, which variables are predictors of pregnancy and live birth in ovarian stimulation?

options.text: AMH and AFC.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend AFC or AMH to predict pregnancy or live birth (strong recommendation).

options.text: Female age and BMI.
options.why: Correct: these are the predictors of pregnancy and live birth the guideline recognises.

options.text: Basal FSH and inhibin B.
options.why: They are on the list of basal markers not recommended to predict pregnancy or live birth.

options.text: Basal oestradiol and progesterone.
options.why: They are also among the basal markers not recommended to predict pregnancy or live birth.

items.explanation: A useful paradox: AFC/AMH predict response but not live birth; age and BMI are not recommended to predict response but are predictors of pregnancy and live birth.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the positions of ESHRE 2025 and NICE 2026 on AMH and live birth after assisted conception?

options.text: Both recommend AMH as a direct predictor of live birth after IVF.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend it for predicting pregnancy or live birth.

options.text: NICE recommends AMH to predict spontaneous pregnancy; ESHRE does not.
options.why: NICE explicitly says not to use AMH to predict pregnancy through spontaneous conception.

options.text: ESHRE does not recommend it for predicting pregnancy or live birth; NICE recommends AMH or AFC as predictors of response to inform decisions and counselling on the likelihood of live birth.
options.why: Correct: it is a nuance, not a head-on contradiction.

options.text: ESHRE recommends AMH to predict live birth; NICE opposes it.
options.why: The emphasis is the other way round: ESHRE does not recommend it for that purpose and NICE uses it for counselling.

items.explanation: ESHRE recommends against using AFC/AMH to predict pregnancy or live birth; NICE recommends using them as response predictors to counsel on the likelihood of live birth. Fewer oocytes means fewer cumulative opportunities, but it does not say which will be competent.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman about to start IVF has a low AMH. She asks: “Does this mean IVF won’t work?” Which answer best fits the evidence?

options.text: Fewer oocytes are likely to be retrieved, but AMH does not say which will be competent and does not mean it won’t work.
options.why: Correct: it distinguishes oocytes retrieved from live birth.

options.text: Yes: with a low AMH the chance of live birth is practically nil.
options.why: AMH as an independent variable is at best weakly predictive of pregnancy; it does not mean “it won’t work”.

options.text: AMH has no relation at all to what will happen in stimulation.
options.why: It does: it is a good predictor of the number of oocytes retrieved.

options.text: Her AMH predicts the outcome better than her age.
options.why: According to ESHRE, age is a predictor of pregnancy and live birth; AMH is not recommended for that.

items.explanation: Oocytes retrieved (biomarker) ≠ clinical pregnancy ≠ live birth. AMH anticipates response; age weighs on the live-birth prognosis.

items.stem: In the Steiner et al. cohort (JAMA 2017), what was the adjusted probability of conceiving by 12 cycles with AMH <0.7 ng/mL versus normal AMH?

options.text: 65% versus 62%.
options.why: Those are the 6-cycle figures, not the 12-cycle ones.

options.text: 50% versus 75%, with a significant difference.
options.why: There were no significant differences; 50–75% was the confidence interval of the low-AMH group at 6 cycles.

options.text: 62% versus 84%, favouring normal AMH.
options.why: It mixes figures and reverses the direction: at 12 cycles it was 84% (low AMH) versus 75% (normal).

options.text: 84% versus 75%, with no significant difference.
options.why: Correct: low AMH was not associated with a lower probability of conceiving.

items.explanation: Steiner 2017: 65% vs 62% by 6 cycles and 84% vs 75% by 12 cycles (AMH <0.7 ng/mL vs normal), with no significant differences. High FSH was not associated with lower fertility either.

items.stem: Which is a genuine limitation when applying the Steiner 2017 results in clinic?

options.text: It was a retrospective study of IVF patients.
options.why: It was a prospective cohort of women without known infertility trying to conceive for ≤3 months.

options.text: The low-AMH subgroup was small (84 women), and the study does not apply to women with already diagnosed infertility.
options.why: Correct: the confidence interval was wide and the population was not infertile.

options.text: It only included women under 30.
options.why: It included women aged 30–44.

options.text: The outcome was live birth, which takes too long to measure.
options.why: The outcome was a positive pregnancy test, not live birth.

items.explanation: Steiner 2017 is an association from a prospective cohort (981 enrolled, 750 analysed), with a small low-AMH group and a “positive test” outcome. It helps reassure women without infertility, not those already diagnosed with it.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with regular cycles has been trying for 14 months; you are starting the infertility work-up. Is an AMH needed to identify the cause?

options.text: Yes: a low AMH would explain her infertility.
options.why: ESHRE notes that, with regular cycles, women with decreased reserve seem to have spontaneous pregnancy rates similar to same-age women with normal reserve, which effectively excludes low reserve per se as a reason for infertility.

options.text: Yes: it helps decide whether expectant management for 12 months is appropriate.
options.why: ESHRE indicates that the studies reviewed do not suggest that reserve determines the probability of spontaneous pregnancy over 6–12 months, so testing may not be informative for that prognosis.

options.text: No: with regular cycles, reserve testing is not required to identify the cause or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months.
options.why: Correct: strong ESHRE 2023 recommendation.

options.text: Not AMH, but a basal FSH, which is more informative.
options.why: Basal FSH is not more informative: a normal FSH does not rule out low reserve, and with regular cycles reserve testing is not needed to identify the cause.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2023: with regular cycles, reserve testing is not required for the aetiological diagnosis or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong, low certainty).

items.stem: On using AMH to forecast spontaneous pregnancy, what do ESHRE, ASRM and NICE say?

options.text: They agree: it does not serve to predict spontaneous conception.
options.why: Correct: all three point the same way (NICE advises against it, ESHRE states it is not required and ASRM says it does not predict current reproductive potential).

options.text: NICE recommends it for that purpose; ESHRE does not.
options.why: NICE explicitly says not to use AMH as a predictor of pregnancy through spontaneous conception.

options.text: ASRM recommends it as a fertility test in women of unproven fertility.
options.why: ASRM says the markers do not predict current reproductive potential in women of unproven fertility and should not be used as a fertility test.

options.text: Only ESHRE addresses it; the others do not.
options.why: ASRM and NICE also address it, in the same direction.

items.explanation: Guideline agreement: NICE (1.18.3) advises against using AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception; ESHRE (strong, low certainty) states that, with regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months; and ASRM says the markers do not predict current reproductive potential in women of unproven fertility.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman, with no current wish to conceive, has a normal AMH: “So I can wait a few years with no problem, right?” What do you answer?

options.text: Yes: a normal AMH guarantees her fertility for the coming years.
options.why: Reserve markers should not be used as a fertility test; they do not predict whether she can wait.

options.text: She should repeat the AMH every year to know when to stop waiting.
options.why: Repeating it does not turn it into a fertility test.

options.text: She also needs a clomiphene challenge test to confirm it.
options.why: Dynamic tests add nothing and should be abandoned.

options.text: AMH estimates how many eggs would respond to treatment, but it does not predict when she will get pregnant or whether she can wait.
options.why: Correct: then you discuss age, plans and history.

items.explanation: Reserve markers should not be used as a fertility test, neither to alarm nor to reassure about the future. What matters for the plan: age, time trying, cycles, history and partner assessment.

items.stem: After explaining to a patient what her AMH cannot tell her, what should you discuss for her reproductive plan?

options.text: A panel of basal FSH, inhibin B and oestradiol.
options.why: These basal hormones are not recommended to predict response or pregnancy.

options.text: Age, time trying, cycles, history and assessment of the partner.
options.why: Correct: these are the elements that do guide the plan.

options.text: Repeating the AMH in another laboratory until it comes back normal.
options.why: Besides not answering the question, values from different assays are not compared directly.

options.text: An immediate IVF referral so as not to lose time.
options.why: An isolated number should not trigger rushed decisions.

items.explanation: Prevent an isolated number from causing distress or rushed decisions: the plan rests on age, time trying, cycles, history and the partner.

items.stem: Which statement reflects ASRM’s position on reserve markers and access to treatment?

options.text: An AMH below the lab range is an exclusion criterion for IVF.
options.why: ASRM says the opposite: extremely low values should not be used to refuse IVF.

options.text: They have no role at all in counselling before IVF.
options.why: They do: with very low reserve fewer oocytes are expected, and that is communicated.

options.text: They should not be used to deny access to infertility treatment, but they do help with counselling.
options.why: Correct: they inform expectations and shared decisions.

options.text: They can deny treatment only if confirmed by a high FSH.
options.why: No combination of markers justifies denying access according to ASRM.

items.explanation: ASRM: reserve markers should not be used to deny access to treatment; they should be used to counsel on expectations and alternatives.

items.stem: A couple with unexplained infertility is offered ovarian stimulation with intrauterine insemination (OS-IUI). The woman has a low AMH and someone proposes excluding her from IUI for that reason. What does ESHRE 2023 say?

options.text: It is uncertain whether reserve determines pregnancy with OS-IUI, and it may be inappropriate to exclude women based on ovarian reserve.
options.why: Correct: that is what the guideline’s justification states.

options.text: Excluding her is correct: low reserve predicts OS-IUI failure.
options.why: ESHRE considers it uncertain whether reserve determines pregnancy with OS-IUI; retrospective studies are conflicting.

options.text: She should go straight to oocyte donation.
options.why: Skipping options because of an AMH value contradicts the principle of not using reserve to deny treatment.

options.text: A clomiphene challenge test is needed before deciding.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve prediction and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2023: it is unclear whether reserve determines pregnancy with OS-IUI, and excluding women from OS-IUI based on reserve may be inappropriate. In IVF, by contrast, ovarian response is a major determinant of cumulative live birth per cycle.

items.stem: Why does ASRM advise against using reserve markers to promote planned oocyte cryopreservation?

options.text: Because AMH cannot be measured reliably before age 35.
options.why: That is not the argument: the problem is what AMH predicts, not the age at measurement.

options.text: Because egg freezing is contraindicated with a low AMH.
options.why: That is not it; the decision to freeze is not based on a lab value used as an alarm.

options.text: Because AMH is only valid in women with PCOS.
options.why: AMH estimates reserve in the general population; the problem is using it as an alarm to freeze.

options.text: Because if they do not predict current reproductive potential, they cannot indicate who “needs” to freeze.
options.why: Correct: that is ASRM’s reasoning.

items.explanation: The decision to freeze is discussed from the person’s reproductive plans and realistic information about the technique, not from an AMH used as an alarm.

items.stem: A company offers its employees an AMH with the message “find out whether you should freeze your eggs”. Which assessment is correct?

options.text: It is an appropriate use: it detects who needs to freeze.
options.why: ASRM says reserve markers should not be used to promote planned egg freezing.

options.text: It uses AMH as a fertility test and as an alarm to freeze, two uses ASRM advises against.
options.why: Correct: it should not be used as a fertility test or to promote cryopreservation.

options.text: It is appropriate only if a basal FSH is added.
options.why: Adding FSH does not change the underlying problem, and isolated FSH is not sensitive.

options.text: It is appropriate if offered only to women aged 20–25, when AMH is most reliable.
options.why: AMH peaking around ages 20–25 does not make it a fertility test.

items.explanation: ASRM: reserve markers should not be used as a fertility test or to promote planned oocyte cryopreservation.

items.stem: Before IVF, a clinic offers a basal FSH as a cheaper alternative to AMH. What does NICE 2026 recommend?

options.text: That it is an acceptable alternative if cost is an issue.
options.why: NICE singles out this very practice as one its recommendations will change, given FSH’s lack of predictive ability.

options.text: Use FSH to predict response, but not live birth.
options.why: NICE advises against FSH for both: response and outcome.

options.text: Do not use FSH as a predictor of ovarian response or of the outcome of assisted conception; use AMH or AFC.
options.why: Correct: NICE NG257 recommendations 1.18.4 and 1.18.5.

options.text: Combine FSH with a clomiphene challenge test to improve accuracy.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve prediction over basal markers and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: NICE 2026: do not use FSH as a predictor of response or of assisted-conception outcome; use AMH or AFC. ESHRE 2025 likewise advises against basal FSH to predict response.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman has a normal basal FSH in the early follicular phase. What can you conclude about her ovarian reserve?

options.text: That a normal FSH does not rule out low reserve; if reserve needs estimating, AFC or AMH are preferred.
options.why: Correct: FSH is specific but not sensitive.

options.text: That her reserve is normal: a normal FSH rules out low reserve.
options.why: Basal FSH is not sensitive: a normal FSH does not rule out low reserve.

options.text: That it must be confirmed with a clomiphene challenge test.
options.why: The clomiphene challenge does not improve prediction and should be abandoned.

options.text: That reserve is normal if FSH is normal again in two cycles.
options.why: Repeating it does not fix its low sensitivity.

items.explanation: Elevated basal FSH: specific, informative. Normal FSH: does not rule out. When reserve truly needs estimating, AFC or AMH.

steps.text: Lucía (fictional case), 34, nulliparous, regular cycles. Her partner is 36. They have been trying for 5 months. A workplace check-up included an AMH reported as “low” by that laboratory's range. She is distressed and asks whether she should freeze her eggs or “go straight to IVF”.
First step: before interpreting the result, ask whether she was taking or recently stopped combined hormonal contraception, whether she had ovarian surgery, and which assay and cut-off the lab used.
Second step: explain what AMH measures (follicle number) and what it does not predict (spontaneous conception in women without known infertility).

Third step: AMH does not indicate that she should freeze or move to IVF. Per NICE, at 34 and without risk factors, investigations are offered after 1 year of unprotected intercourse; referral is brought forward from age 36 or if either partner has a known cause or predisposing factors.

Twist: months later, with a full work-up and an indication for IVF, even if the AMH turned out to be extremely low, AMH (or AFC) does help: it anticipates her response to stimulation and adjusts counselling, without being used to refuse treatment.
Communication: acknowledge her distress, explain the uncertainty honestly and avoid letting an isolated number become a diagnosis.

asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.title: Testing and interpreting measures of ovarian reserve: a committee opinion
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.population: Women with and without known infertility assessed with ovarian reserve markers.
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.finding: AMH and AFC predict oocyte yield in IVF well but are poor independent predictors of reproductive potential; they should not be used as a fertility test, to deny treatment, or to promote planned oocyte cryopreservation.
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.limitations: Committee opinion (not a GRADE guideline); US context.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.title: Ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI — ESHRE guideline update 2025
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Ovarian Stimulation
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.population: Women starting ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI.
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.finding: Recommends AFC or AMH to predict high and low response (strong). Does not recommend AFC, AMH or other basal markers to predict pregnancy or live birth (strong). Female age and BMI are predictors of pregnancy and live birth (strong). Age, BMI, basal FSH, inhibin B, basal oestradiol, basal progesterone and basal LH are not recommended to predict response (strong).
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.limitations: Full guideline v23 (September 2026); journal version: Hum Reprod 2026;41(4):498-514. Certainty for each recommendation is given in the full guideline.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

steiner-2017-jama.title: Association Between Biomarkers of Ovarian Reserve and Infertility Among Older Women of Reproductive Age
steiner-2017-jama.authors: Steiner AZ, Pritchard D, Stanczyk FZ, et al.
steiner-2017-jama.population: Prospective time-to-pregnancy cohort: women aged 30–44 with no history of infertility, trying to conceive for ≤3 months (North Carolina, USA); 981 enrolled, 750 analysed.
steiner-2017-jama.finding: AMH <0.7 ng/mL was not associated with a lower probability of conceiving by 6 cycles (65% vs 62%) or 12 cycles (84% vs 75%) versus normal AMH; neither was high FSH. Conception defined as a positive pregnancy test.
steiner-2017-jama.limitations: Outcome = positive pregnancy test, not live birth; observational; excludes known infertility; few women with low AMH (<0.7 ng/mL; n=84).

teede-2023-pcos-guideline.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.; International PCOS Network
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.finding: Graded recommendations (GRADE strength and certainty) on diagnosis (including AMH), glycaemic assessment, lifestyle, diet, metformin, inositol and ovulation induction with letrozole.
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.limitations: Many recommendations with low or very low certainty; practice points and consensus recommendations carry no certainty rating.
